Additional Sessions Judge Shimla, Camp at Rohru in Cr. Appeal No. 7-R/10 of 2005 dated
14.11.2008 vide which, learned appellate court has upheld the judgment of conviction passed by the
Court of learned Sub Divisional Judicial Magistrate, Rohru in Cr. Case No. 65-3 of 2004 dated
7.12.2004, whereby the petitioner was convicted by learned trial court for commission of offence
punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(ii) read with Section 7(iii) of Prevention of Food Whether

was convicted.
2.

The case of the prosecution was that on 22.4.2004 Food Inspector L.D. Thakur inspected the premises i.e. Chanchal Singh Sweets Shop, Rohru at about 10:00 a.m. and found the present petitioner conducting business of said sweet shop.
The of items which were kept for sale to the general public included "burfi, mutter, besan burfi, namkeen" etc.

Food Inspector asked rt the petitioner to produce P.F.A. licence issued in his favour for sale of food articles, as was required under Rule 50 of P.F.A. Rules, 1955, however, accused failed to produce any licence issued in his favour to conduct the abovementioned business for the years 2003-2005.
Besides this, the sweets were kept uncovered exposed to rain, dust and flies.
Accordingly, Food Inspector prepared a spot map which was duly signed by the accused and Food Inspector himself.

Thereafter, Food Inspector placed documents of the accused before Chief Medical Officer, Shimla who was empowered to give written consent under Section 20 of the P.F.A. Act to launch prosecution against the accused.

In this background, Food Inspector filed complaint against the accused under Section 16(1)(a)(ii) of P.F.A.
Act.
3.

As a prima facie case was made out against the accused for commission of offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(II) read with Section 7(iii) of P.F.A. Act, 1954, accordingly notice of accusation was put to him to which accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

. 
4. On the basis of material produced on record by the prosecution, learned trial court held that the prosecution was able to prove its case against the accused beyond all reasonable doubt for commission of offence punishable under Sections 16(1)(a)(II) read with Section 7(iii) of P.F.A. Act,
1954 and of sentenced him to undergo simple imprisonment for 03 months and to pay fine of `500/-.
5. rtFeeling aggrieved by the said judgment passed by learned trial court, accused preferred an appeal before learned appellate court.
Learned appellate court upheld the judgment of conviction and sentence imposed upon the present petitioner by the learned trial court and dismissed the appeal.
6. Feeling aggrieved by the said two judgments passed by learned courts below, the accused has preferred the present revision petition.
7. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and have also gone through the records of the case as well as the judgments passed by both the learned courts below.

sentences.text: It stands established on the basis of material produced on record by the prosecution that on 22.4.2004, when Food Inspector L.D. Thakur inspected the Chanchal Singh Sweets Shop at Rohru wherein the present petitioner was conducting the business of sweet shop, he was not possessing any licence for sale of food articles which were being sold in the shop as is the requirement under Rule 50 of P.F.A. Rules, 1955.

It is duly borne .
out from the records that the complainant was duly appointed as Food Inspector on the relevant date and was competent to inspect the premises of the accused as well as to launch prosecution in case sanction was duly accorded by the competent authority.

It further stands proved on record by the of prosecution that Chief Medical Officer, Shimla was competent to accord written consent for the purposes of launching prosecution rt as is contemplated under Section 20 of the P.F.A. Act and it was on the basis of the written consent accorded in this regard by Chief Medical Officer, Shimla that the prosecution was launched against the accused by the complainant.

It is apparent and evident from the findings returned by learned trial court as well as by learned appellate court that the petitioner in fact was conducting his business of sweet shop in violation of the provisions of P.F.A. Act, as he was not having any valid licence as on 22.4.2004.
The findings returned in this regard by both learned courts below could not be proved to be either perverse or contrary to the records by the learned counsel for the petitioner.
The factum of the prosecution not possessing a valid licence as on 22.4.2004 to conduct the business of sweet shop could not be refuted by the learned counsel for the petitioner.

His contention that the learned trial court had brushed aside non compliance of Section 10(7) of the P.F.A. Act and that non association of an independent witness had vitiated the entire proceedings and had resulted in miscarriage of justice is without .
any merit.

This is for the reason that the factum of the petitioner conducting the business of sweet shop without any valid licence is an established fact and even otherwise to demonstrate this fact the provisions of Sub Section 7 of Section 10 of P.F.A. Act, 1954 have no relevance.

It is not a case where any sample was of taken because in the present case the allegation against the petitioner was that he was running the business without a valid rt licence and this fact stands duly proved by the prosecution because the onus to have proved that he was having a valid licence to conduct the business of sweet shop could have been easily discharged by the petitioner by producing a licence issued in his favour by the competent authority before the Food Inspector which he did not produce,
as he was not having any valid licence as on 22.4.2004 to conduct the said business.

9. A perusal of the judgments passed by both learned courts below demonstrate that all these aspects have been taken into consideration by both learned courts below and it cannot be said that the conclusions which have been arrived at by both learned courts below on the basis of material produced on record by the prosecution were either perverse or were not borne out from the material on record.

Even during the course of arguments, learned counsel for the petitioner could not point out as to what was the perversity with the findings returned by both learned courts below or which particular finding returned either by learned trial court or by learned appellate court was not borne .
out from the records of the case.

Lastly it was argued by the learned counsel for the petitioner that the petitioner has suffered pain and agony of trial for more than 12 years and it was prayed that keeping in view the fact that the petitioner is 65 years of age as of now, the of sentence of imprisonment of the petitioner be commuted to fine and in this regard reliance was placed by the learned counsel for rt the petitioner on the following decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court:-
(i) In Haripada Das v. State of West Bangal and another, 1998 (2) FAC 187, the Apex Curt has held:-
"Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and also considering that the appellant was released on bail by this Court long back and because of the protracted litigation up to this court he has also suffered a lot of mental agony and also financial hardship and also considering the fact that he had already undergone imprisonment for more than three weeks, we feel that in the facts of the case the ends of the justice will be met if the sentence of imprisonment is reduced to the period already undergone.

sentences.text: the appellant has been awarded six months simple imprisonment and has also been ordered to pay a fine of Rs. 1000/-.
Under clause (d) of Section 433 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the appropriate government is empowered to commute the sentence of simple imprisonment for fine.
We think that this would be an appropriate case for commutation of sentence where almost a decade has gone by.

We, therefore, direct the appellant to deposit in the trial court a sum of Rs. 6000/- as find in commutation of the sentence of six months simple imprisonment within a period of six weeks from today and intimate to the appropriate government that such fine has been deposited.

On deposit of such fine,
the State Government may formalize he matter by passing appropriate orders under clause (d) of Section 433 of the code of Criminal Procedure."

(iii) Santosh Kumar v. Municipal Corporation and another, 2000(2) .
FAC 76 wherein it was held:-

sentences.text: We, therefore, direct the appellant to deposit in the trial court a sum of Rupees 10,000/- as fined in commutation of the of sentence of 6 months imprisonment within a period of 6 weeks from today and intimate to the appropriate Government that such fine has been deposited.
On deposit of the fine the State Government may formalize the matter by passing appropriate order under clause (d) of Section 433 of the code of Criminal Procedure.
In the meanwhile the appellant will remain on bail."
rt 11.

Applying the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in this case, admittedly the offence was committed more than 12 years ago and the petitioner was in fact subsequently issued a licence to carry out business in the name and style of Chanchal Sweets Shop Near SBI Rohru on 13.5.2004 which is on record as Ext. P1, and further it is not a case where the sweets being sold by the petitioner were found to be extraneous or injurious to health
, it would be appropriate if the sentence of the petitioner is commuted to fine.

Accordingly, the petitioner is directed to deposit a fine of `50,000/- in the trial court in commutation of unserved sentence of imprisonment within four weeks from today and to intimate the Government that such fine has been deposited.
On the fine being deposited, the State Government may formalize the matter by passing an appropriate order under clause (d) of Section 433 of Criminal Procedure Code.

12. In the meantime, the sentence awarded to the .
petitioner is suspended for a period of two months on his furnishing personal bond in the sum of `25,000/- with one surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned trial court.
The petition stands disposed of accordingly.
